Getting started with zupix

Source: vignettes/articles/zupix.Rmd
zupix.Rmd
library(zupix)
f <- system.file("extdata", "gradient.png", package = "zupix")

zupix decodes PNG, JPEG, WebP and QOI, and encodes the same four, with every codec compiled into the package. This article goes through the shapes it reads into, the metadata it reports, the writers, the limits that guard against hostile files, the C interface for other packages, how fast it is, and where its output differs from the reference decoders.

Three shapes

pix_read() returns one of three shapes, chosen with as.

A nativeRaster (the default) is 8-bit RGBA packed one pixel per integer, as png::readPNG(native = TRUE) returns it. It is the smallest shape and draws directly with grid::grid.raster() or graphics::rasterImage().

native <- pix_read(f)
class(native)
#> [1] "nativeRaster"
dim(native)
#> [1] 32 48

A double array holds values in [0, 1], as png::readPNG() returns them: height x width x channels, or a matrix for a grey image.

dbl <- pix_read(f, as = "double")
dim(dbl)
#> [1] 32 48  3
range(dbl)
#> [1] 0 1

An integer array holds the sample values themselves, with their depth in a bits attribute: 0..255 at 8 bits, 0..65535 at 16.

int <- pix_read(f, as = "integer")
attr(int, "bits")
#> [1] 8

bits forces a depth, and channels adds channels: grey becomes RGB, and an opaque alpha can be added. Removing a channel is refused, because turning colour into grey or dropping transparency is a colour decision zupix leaves to you.

dim(pix_read(f, as = "integer", channels = 4L))
#> [1] 32 48  4
attr(pix_read(f, as = "integer", bits = 16L), "bits")
#> [1] 16
pix_read(f, as = "integer", channels = 1L)
#> Error in `pix_read()`:
#> ! `channels` would remove channels the image has.

Metadata

pix_info() reads an image’s header and metadata without decoding pixels: format, size, depth, colour type, transparency, interlacing, animation, density, EXIF orientation, PNG’s colour chunks, and whether an ICC profile or EXIF data is present. It takes any number of paths and returns a row for each.

pix_info(f)
#>   format width height bits colour_type alpha interlaced animated density_x
#> 1    png    48     32    8         rgb FALSE      FALSE    FALSE        NA
#>   density_y density_unit orientation gamma srgb chrm cicp   icc  exif
#> 1        NA           NA          NA    NA   NA NULL NULL FALSE FALSE
#>   qoi_linear
#> 1         NA

pix_icc() and pix_exif() return the ICC profile and the EXIF block as raw vectors, or NULL. zupix never applies a profile: pass it to a colour-management package.

The EXIF orientation says how a camera was held. Pixels come back as stored; pix_read(orient = TRUE) or pix_orient() rotates or flips them losslessly.

small <- int[1:2, 1:3, 1]
small
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    0    5   11
#> [2,]    0    5   11
pix_orient(small, 6L) # 90 degrees clockwise
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    0    0
#> [2,]    5    5
#> [3,]   11   11

Animated PNG and WebP decode their first frame, with an animated attribute set to TRUE.

Writing

pix_write() picks the format from the file’s extension. Each format also has its own writer with its own options.

out <- tempfile(fileext = ".webp")
pix_write(int, out, lossless = TRUE)
identical(pix_read(out, as = "integer"), int)
#> [1] TRUE
  • pix_write_png() writes 8 or 16 bits with 1 to 4 channels, at a zlib compression from 0 to 9, with an optional ICC profile, EXIF block or sRGB rendering intent.
  • pix_write_jpeg() takes a quality on libjpeg’s scale, a chroma subsampling and progressive. JPEG stores no alpha: an alpha channel is dropped only when every pixel is opaque.
  • pix_write_webp() is lossy or lossless, with a method trading speed for size.
  • pix_write_qoi() writes 8-bit RGB or RGBA.

The writers take every shape pix_read() returns. Doubles are clamped to [0, 1] and rounded; an integer array without a bits attribute is treated as 8-bit if every value is at most 255. Without a file, the writers return the encoded bytes as a raw vector.

png <- pix_write_png(int, icc = as.raw(1:100))
length(png)
#> [1] 311
identical(pix_icc(png), as.raw(1:100))
#> [1] TRUE

Limits and errors

A small file can declare a huge image. zupix parses the header, checks it against pix_limits(), and allocates only then. The limits are the largest side, the number of pixels, the bytes one decode may use, and the bytes of metadata.

pix_limits()
#> <zupix_limits>
#>   max_side      65,535
#>   max_pixels    100,000,000
#>   max_bytes     2,147,483,648
#>   max_metadata  16,777,216

Every error is a condition of class zupix_error with one more specific class, such as zupix_limit_error, zupix_decode_error (a corrupt or truncated file; zupix never returns a partial image) or zupix_unsupported_error (a valid feature outside zupix’s scope, such as 12-bit or arithmetic-coded JPEG). Handle them by class; ?zupix-conditions lists them all.

truncated <- readBin(f, "raw", 100)
tryCatch(
  pix_read(truncated),
  zupix_decode_error = function(e) "corrupt or truncated"
)
#> [1] "corrupt or truncated"

From C

Other packages can call the same codecs from C, without going through R. Declare Imports: zupix and LinkingTo: zupix, import any function of zupix in your NAMESPACE so its DLL is loaded first, and include zupix-r.h:

#include <zupix-r.h>

SEXP my_image_width(SEXP bytes) {
  const zupix_api_v1 *api = zupix_api();
  zpx_info info = {sizeof info};
  if (api == NULL) Rf_error("zupix speaks another ABI version");
  if (api->probe(RAW(bytes), XLENGTH(bytes), NULL, &info) != ZPX_OK)
    return Rf_ScalarInteger(NA_INTEGER);
  return Rf_ScalarInteger((int) info.width);
}

The table also decodes into five pixel layouts with any row stride, extracts ICC and EXIF data, and encodes all four formats through a callback. Nothing in it calls R or raises an R error. Looking the table up does: if zupix is not loaded, the first zupix_api() raises an R error, so make that call from a .Call entry point, as above. inst/include/zupix.h documents every function.

Speed

Measured on a 12-megapixel synthetic photograph (R 4.5.2, macOS, x86_64), against the packages that link the same formats’ system libraries. Times are medians; lower is faster.

Operation Reference zupix
PNG decode to nativeRaster png 0.19 s 0.22 s
JPEG decode to nativeRaster jpeg 0.18 s 0.06 s
WebP decode webp 2.52 s (doubles) 0.25 s (nativeRaster)
PNG encode, level 6 png 2.25 s 2.82 s, same size
JPEG encode, quality 90 jpeg 0.57 s 0.86 s
WebP encode, quality 75 webp 1.84 s 1.52 s
pix_info() on 1,000 files 0.18 s

PNG decoding spends about the same time in the decoder as libpng; the rest is reading the whole file into memory first. zupix’s JPEG decoder is Wuffs, and its JPEG encoder is libjpeg-turbo without SIMD.

Where zupix differs from the reference decoders

zupix is tested against reference decoders on public test suites. It decodes every valid PngSuite image exactly as the png package does, and every JPEG it was tested on exactly as libjpeg-turbo does. The jpeg package bundles IJG libjpeg 9e, which upsamples colour differently, so colour JPEGs read with it differ from zupix’s by a few levels near sharp edges.

One difference comes from the version of Wuffs zupix bundles (v0.4.0-alpha.12): on 8 of the 131 files in libwebp’s test suite, lossy WebP colour decodes up to 32 levels away from libwebp’s output, though lossy WebP is specified to decode exactly. Alpha, and lossless WebP, are exact. The tests pin these files, so an update of Wuffs that fixes them shows up.

QOI decodes through the format’s reference decoder, qoi.h, and matches it exactly on every QOI test image.
